content_html:
Probabilistic Brain

The brain handles uncertainty at multiple levels: synaptic transmission is probabilistic; neural populations encode likelihoods; hippocampal CA3 supports pattern completion from partial cues; cortical circuits integrate noisy evidence in a diffusion-like manner; and hierarchical predictive coding combines priors with incoming sensory data. These mechanisms make recall a reconstruction — the most probable pattern given cues and prior knowledge.

Implication for memory: Because encoding, storage, and retrieval are built atop probabilistic synapses, population codes, and Bayesian-like updates, recall is a best-guess reconstruction conditioned on current cues and prior experience.

Synaptic transmission is probabilistic

Release of neurotransmitter vesicles occurs with probability < 1.0 and varies across boutons and conditions. This variability shapes synaptic strength and learning rules.

Population coding & uncertainty

Neural ensembles encode stimuli as probability distributions; variability and noise correlations carry information about uncertainty and are exploited by downstream decoders.

Hippocampal CA3 pattern completion (reconstructive recall)

Recurrent collaterals in CA3 enable retrieval of coherent representations from degraded inputs—pattern completion—a core reason recall behaves like inference.

Decision-making as stochastic evidence accumulation

Activity in parietal/frontal circuits reflects noisy accumulation toward a bound (drift–diffusion), aligning with observed reaction time and choice variability.

Predictive coding / Free-energy: priors × likelihood

Hierarchical cortical circuits combine prior expectations with incoming likelihoods to minimize prediction error—formally a Bayesian update process.
